stem: A farmer keeps beef cattle on natural grazing in an area of moderate rainfall and wants to improve the feed available for his herd.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the vegetation of natural grazing land and its value to livestock.

points.description: Grasses: the main source of energy and fibre; grow fast in the rains.
Grass quality falls (less protein, more fibre) as it matures and in the dry season.
Legumes: high in protein and calcium, and fix nitrogen.
Browse (leaves and pods of trees and shrubs): green, protein-rich feed into the dry season, especially for goats.

parts.explanation: Grasses, legumes and browse with their value.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how an improved grass-legume pasture should be established.

points.description: Choose a suitable site, test the soil and lime if acid (legumes need near-neutral soil).
Clear and plough, then harrow to a fine, firm seedbed because pasture seeds are small.
Choose species suited to the climate and soil; buy certified seed and inoculate legume seed with Rhizobium so it fixes nitrogen.
Apply phosphorus at sowing; sow shallowly at the start of the rains and roll to firm the soil around the seed.
Control weeds while the pasture establishes and graze lightly only when plants are firmly rooted.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Discuss whether the farmer should use rotational grazing and controlled burning on the rest of the natural grazing.

points.description: Rotational grazing rests each area so grasses recover, set seed and build reserves; good perennial grasses survive.
It gives more even use, breaks worm cycles and allows dry-season reserves, but needs fencing, water in each camp and planning.
Controlled burning removes old, unpalatable grass, stimulates fresh regrowth and checks bush encroachment.
Burning must be planned: only where old grass has built up, in calm weather, with fireguards, followed by rest.
Burning too often or uncontrolled fires leave soil bare, cause erosion and destroy dry-season feed, fences and property.
Judgement: rotation should be adopted with correct stocking; burning used occasionally and carefully as a tool, not a routine.

explanation: Describe grazing vegetation, explain pasture establishment and evaluate rotational grazing and burning.

stem: A smallholder keeps a herd of dairy goats. Last season 6 of the 40 kids born died within their first month, many after diarrhoea.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe **four** signs the smallholder could use to recognise ill-health in a goat.

points.description: Dull, standing apart from the herd, head low.
Loss of appetite / stops chewing the cud.
Abnormal body temperature (fever, above about 39-40 °C) / fast breathing.
Diarrhoea, discharges from eyes or nose, rough coat, pale membranes or a fall in milk yield.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of kids that died.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how infectious diarrhoea can spread among young kids and why colostrum helps protect them.

points.description: Pathogens in the dung of sick kids contaminate the floor, bedding, teats, feed and water; other kids swallow them.
Spread is faster in crowded, wet, dirty pens and on shared equipment.
Colostrum gives ready-made antibodies (passive immunity) if sucked within the first few hours, protecting the gut until the kid's own immunity develops.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Discuss the measures the smallholder could take to reduce kid deaths next season, and whether they are worth the cost.

points.description: Make sure every kid sucks colostrum within the first few hours (or is fed stored colostrum).
Kid in clean, dry, draught-free pens with fresh bedding; clean and disinfect pens and feeding equipment regularly.
Isolate sick kids at once and seek veterinary advice; give fluids to scouring kids as advised.
Feed does well in late pregnancy and supply clean water, so kids are strong and milk is plentiful.
Vaccinate and deworm does as advised; avoid overcrowding; quarantine new goats.

Judgement: most measures (colostrum, hygiene, isolation) cost little labour and money compared with the value of the kids lost, so they are worth it; housing improvements cost more but repay over several seasons.
